title: Map: yt-transcript — a Node CLI for YouTube transcripts
description:
## Destination

A **spec ticket** describing the `yt-transcript` Node CLI — invocation, Markdown output contract, catalog, and playlist behaviour — together with `CONTEXT.md`, any ADRs, and the agent procedure doc, such that **one implementer session** can build it end to end.

## Notes

**Domain:** turning YouTube videos the user has no time to watch into Markdown transcripts usable as agent input or reference material. Explicitly **not** summaries.

**Skills every session should consult:** `grilling` and `domain-modeling`. Write `CONTEXT.md` lazily and inline as terms resolve; offer ADRs only for decisions that are hard to reverse, surprising, and the result of a real trade-off.

**No LLM in the final application.** Every rule the tool applies at runtime must be deterministic and mechanical — regex, position, counting. Cleaning decisions that would need semantic judgement are not available; a rule that cannot be written syntactically must be dropped or made to fail safe.

### Settled during charting — do NOT re-ask the user

- **Shape:** a Node.js application, run locally via `npx` (not published to npm; structured so publishing stays a later option). Command name: `yt-transcript`.
- **No PowerShell.** `Get-Transcript.ps1` is retired; there is no `scripts/` folder. The repo *is* the application — standard Node layout.
- **Fetching (settled, see Decisions):** the CLI spawns the **`yt-dlp` binary** as a child process, preflight-checking for it on PATH and failing with a clear, actionable message if absent. Always pass **`--js-runtimes node`** — it costs nothing, silences the deprecation warning, and keeps the pipeline working if subtitles ever do start requiring a JS runtime. Pure-JS fetching was investigated and **rejected as not durable**; do not re-open it. Full evidence: `archive/research/yt-dlp-js-runtime-and-pure-js-paths.md`.
- **Input:** accepts a YouTube URL **or** a bare video id. Must tolerate `youtube.com/watch?v=`, `youtu.be/`, `/shorts/`, and trailing `?si=` / `&t=` junk.
- **Output:** one Markdown file per video in a **flat** `transcripts/` directory, named in kebab-case from the video title.
- **Frontmatter (settled, see Decisions):** exactly seven keys in fixed order — `title`, `url`, `channel`, `duration`, `upload_date`, `fetched`, `subtitles` (`manual` | `auto`). No separate `video_id` — the URL carries it.
- **Subtitles (settled, see Decisions):** one blind `yt-dlp --write-sub --write-auto-sub --sub-langs <lang>` per video — yt-dlp itself prefers the manual track, so there is no pre-flight and no track ranking of our own. Default language `en`, overridable, matched **exactly** (`en` does not match `en-US`). `manual` vs `auto` is read from the VTT body (`<c>` word-timing tags ⇒ auto), never from the log.
- **Paragraphing (settled, see Decisions):** break at the next **sentence end** once the paragraph reaches **100 words**; `PARAGRAPH_MIN_WORDS = 100`, hard-coded, not a flag. **Timing is not used at all** — cue gaps are exactly 0.000s in every sample, so no pause threshold can fire, and word-level timing proved speaker-dependent. Do not re-open the 2.0s/0.8s pause idea. The sentence signal is YouTube's own ASR punctuation.
- **Catalog (settled, see Decisions):** `transcripts/README.md`, a Markdown table **derived** from the transcript files' frontmatter so it cannot drift, rebuilt by full rescan.
- **Single entry point.** No script invoking another script; one CLI with flags/subcommands.
- **`package.json` is required** with `"type": "module"` and `"engines": { "node": ">=22" }` — v22 is yt-dlp's floor for `--js-runtimes node`, and this machine runs v24. The cleaner currently relies on Node's ESM auto-detection, and `fnm --use-on-cd` makes the active Node version variable by design. Specify this; it is not a ticket.
- **Defence in depth:** when spawning `yt-dlp`, strip any `fnm_multishells` entries from the child process PATH. The root cause is fixed on this machine, but the guard keeps the tool portable.
- **Existing artifacts:** 7 `.vtt` files and their `_cleaned.txt` siblings sit at the repo root, plus strays (an `.srt`, a `-transcript.txt`, a file whose name begins with `--`). The cleaned text is migrated into `transcripts/` with real titles; the `.vtt` intermediates are deleted as regenerable. This is hand-off execution, not a decision.

### Tracker mechanics (verified against br 0.6.0)

- Use `--description-file`, **never** `-d/--description` — a `"` in the text breaks shell quoting and spills a positional argument.
- Colons in labels are accepted (`wayfinder:map`).
- `--parent` creates hierarchy but does **not** block. Blocking is `br dep add <issue> <depends-on>` (default type `blocks`).
- **Frontier query:** `br ready --json`. Blocked work: `br blocked --json`.
- Run `br sync --flush-only` after mutations. **This repo IS under git** (branch `develop`; `.beads/` is tracked), so follow the issue-tracker doc: `br sync --flush-only && git add .beads/` before any commit that touches bead state.
- **Deleted issues persist in `issues.jsonl` as `"status":"tombstone"` rows** (with `deleted_at` / `deleted_by`). This is **correct** — tombstones are how deletions propagate to other clones. Do not try to strip them; `br sync` will refuse, and removing them by hand would let deleted issues resurrect.

## Decisions so far

- [yt-dlp-ejs and pure-JS viability](ytdlp-sab.5): Keep spawning the `yt-dlp` binary — pure-JS (`youtubei.js` and friends) is not durable against YouTube's countermeasures. `yt-dlp-ejs` is a challenge-solver, not a runtime, and is **not needed for subtitles**: verified live that `--write-auto-sub` output is byte-identical (122,555 bytes) with and without a JS runtime. Pass `--js-runtimes node` anyway as free insurance. Report: `archive/research/yt-dlp-js-runtime-and-pure-js-paths.md`

- [Tune the paragraph-break threshold](ytdlp-sab.1): Break at the next sentence end past **100 words**, hard-coded as `PARAGRAPH_MIN_WORDS`. The ticket's premise was falsified — inter-cue gaps are **exactly 0.000s** in all 8 files, so the shipped 2.0s rule has never once fired and 0.8s was equally dead. Word-level timing is speaker-dependent (15/19/125 breaks at one threshold; 696-word worst paragraph); sentence length is stable at 15.5–19.2 words across all 8. The word cap, framed as an optional backstop, turned out to be the primary signal. Transfers to manual subs unchanged. Prototype: branch `prototype/paragraph-rules`.

- [Markdown output and filename contract](ytdlp-sab.2): Slug = NFKD-fold, lowercase, delete apostrophes, non-alphanumeric runs to `-`, trim ends; **120-char** cap truncated at a `-` boundary; empty slug falls back to the video id. Verified against all 8 real titles. Frontmatter is exactly 7 keys in fixed order, with `title`/`channel`/`duration` **always double-quoted** (a bare `duration: 41:18` parses as sexagesimal `2478`; `title: /wayfinder: …` is invalid YAML), `upload_date` as `YYYY-MM-DD`, `fetched` a UTC instant, `url` normalised to `https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=<id>`. Body is plain prose — **no H1, no timestamps**. **Identity is the frontmatter `url`, not the filename**: re-run overwrites silently and bumps `fetched`; a true title collision suffixes the second file with the video id. Re-fetching is **user-driven only** — there is no proactive staleness policy and the catalog, being derived, follows automatically. (This closed the *Transcript freshness* fog patch.)

- [Catalog contents and rebuild semantics](ytdlp-sab.3): The catalog is **`transcripts/README.md`** — the folder README, so the scan rule **"any `.md` with parseable frontmatter is a transcript"** excludes it with no filename special-case. Five columns in order: **Title** (linked to the transcript's relative path), **Channel**, **Duration**, **Uploaded**, **Subtitles**; `url` and `fetched` are deliberately not surfaced. Sort **`upload_date` descending, tie-break `title` ascending** — both immutable, so a re-fetch never reorders a row. Rebuild fires **both** automatically after every successful fetch **and** explicitly via the **`yt-transcript catalog` subcommand** (not a flag, not a second executable), and is **always a full rescan**. **Narrowed by [Playlist and channel handling](ytdlp-sab.4):** the automatic rebuild fires after every successful *single-video* fetch and **once at the end of a batch**, never once per video. Above the table: `# Transcripts`, then `N transcripts, regenerated by yt-transcript catalog`. A malformed transcript is **skipped with a warning naming the file and telling the user to re-download it** — never silent, never fatal. Titles are `|`-escaped in the catalog cell only; zero transcripts yields the count line and no table. **Derivability is the standing acceptance test for any future column:** computable from the seven frontmatter keys plus the file path, or it does not belong.

- [Playlist and channel handling](ytdlp-sab.4): A playlist or channel URL **expands** into a **batch** of fetches; a fetch is still one video, one `yt-dlp` invocation. Detection is **purely syntactic** (yt-dlp picks its extractor by regex before any network I/O), and `watch?v=…&list=…` means **the video** — a deliberate divergence from yt-dlp, which takes the whole playlist, so `--no-playlist` must be passed; `--playlist` forces the batch reading. A bare `@handle` is rewritten to the channel's **Videos tab** (yt-dlp would expand it to Videos + Shorts + Live). **Skipping is batch-only** — a single video URL still overwrites; a batch expands first (2 HTTP requests for 50 items), normalises to the settled `url` form, and subtracts what `transcripts/` already holds, using the same full scan the catalog rebuild performs. `--force` means exactly "ignore the skip set". Failures **continue, collect, report**, exit non-zero if any failed; **HTTP 429 is the one retried exception** (3 attempts, 5s/15s/45s, labelled *rate-limited*), because the no-retry rule was reasoned from permanence. Success requires exit 0 **and** a non-empty subtitle file — a missing language exits 0 silently. **Confirmed by [Missing subtitles in the requested language](ytdlp-sab.6):** measured directly — no captions exits **0** with `There are no subtitles for the requested languages`, an HTTP 429 exits **1**. The settled success test holds, and the exit code alone separates the permanent failure from the retryable one. Expansion failure is a hard error; zero videos, and an all-skipped batch, are successes. **No cap**, but a **one-second delay between fetches** in batch mode, done by our own loop since every yt-dlp sleep flag acts inside one invocation. **Playlist provenance is not recorded** — the playlist is how you found the video, not what the video is. Evidence: `archive/research/yt-dlp-playlist-and-channel-urls.md`

- [Missing subtitles in the requested language](ytdlp-sab.6): **The requested language is the output language, always** — no cross-language fallback, because the settled seven-key frontmatter has nowhere to record one. But the ticket's premise was largely unreachable: YouTube **auto-translates auto captions into ~160 languages**, so a video with any auto captions has the requested language (verified: `--sub-langs zu` began downloading Zulu). Auto-translation is **accepted, not refused** — a machine-translated English track records as plain `subtitles: auto`, and the frontmatter contract is **not** reopened (though it proved largely moot: translated tracks **reliably 429**, see *Translated tracks are rate-limited into uselessness*); the deliberate cost is that a transcript cannot distinguish English ASR from English translated from Spanish. Fetch is **one blind invocation**, `--write-sub --write-auto-sub --sub-langs en`: yt-dlp writes a single file and prefers the manual track by itself (verified on a TED talk carrying both), so "prefer manual" needs no code. `en-orig` is never requested — byte-identical to `en` (351,425 bytes) on an English-original video. `live_chat` is excluded (yt-dlp's own `all,-live_chat` idiom); it is the only "manual" track a live stream has. **`manual` vs `auto` is read from the VTT body** — auto carries `<c>` word-timing tags and `align:start position:0%`, manual carries neither (0 vs 319–1265 across the 8 samples); `Kind: captions` appears in both and is useless, and the log says `Writing video subtitles to:` for auto tracks too. The rule is **unverified against auto-*translated* tracks**, which could not be downloaded at all — but that same 429 wall means every reachable input falls into one of the two verified classes. **No usable subtitles at all is a hard error**: exit 1, no file, no catalog rebuild; in a batch it is an ordinary failure-summary entry, permanent and not retried. **No stderr parsing is needed to classify the failure:** measured directly, no captions exits **0** with `There are no subtitles for the requested languages` and no file, while an HTTP 429 exits **1** — so the exit code alone tells the permanent failure from the retryable one, and the success test settled in [Playlist and channel handling](ytdlp-sab.4) stands unchanged.

- [Dedup safety on manually-authored subtitles](ytdlp-sab.7): **Dedup runs only on `auto` tracks** — on a manual track the overlap is forced to 0. Measured over 5 live-fetched manual VTTs (1504 cues): **13 deletions, all 13 false positives, zero true positives**, about one corruption per 115 cues. `getOverlapSize` has **no minimum `k`** and compares against the *whole accumulated paragraph*, so a sentence opening on the word the last one closed with (`…like that.` + `That would be…`), a discourse marker, a dialogue echo, or a rhetorical repeat (`…do you?` + `Do you?` — the whole cue erased) all lose real speech. **Retuning cannot fix it:** manual false positives reach **k=7**, inside auto's densest band (2001 at k=6, 3942 at k=7), so a cutoff that kills them discards ~40% of genuine auto overlaps. The classifier is **free** — the `<c>` rule from [Missing subtitles in the requested language](ytdlp-sab.6) is computed anyway for the `subtitles` frontmatter key, same signal, second consumer. **Ordering consequence for the spec:** classification becomes a *precondition of cleaning*, not a labelling step — the pipeline is load → classify → clean. Auto tracks show low-`k` matches too (~0.5% of auto matches), plausibly the same false positives masked by the rolling window; **noted, deliberately not ticketed**. Prototype: branch `prototype/dedup-safety`.


- [Translated tracks are rate-limited into uselessness](ytdlp-sab.9): **Nothing is special-cased — every settled rule stands unchanged.** The tool retrieves **English**; manual, ASR or machine-translated are all acceptable output, and the **original language is never surfaced, never named in an error, and never suggested as `--lang <orig>`**. That scope decision removes the audience for every remedy the ticket proposed. So: a translated-track 429 is **not distinguished** from an ordinary one (it *cannot* be — the `-J` pre-flight is dropped by decision, so both are the same observable: non-zero exit, `HTTP Error 429`, no file); the **retry ladder is unchanged** (3 attempts, 5s/15s/45s), accepting ~65s spent on a non-English video fetched with the default `--lang en`; the user sees **exit 1** and the existing rate-limited message naming the video, with **no second exit code**. Rejected: an eager `-J` pre-flight (taxes every fetch to serve a path nobody wants), a **lazy `--list-subs` probe** after the retries (free on the happy path, but its only payoff is the discarded original-language diagnosis), **refusing to request translated tracks at all** (a machine-translated English track is exactly the wanted output when obtainable — declining to ask converts a sometimes-succeeding path into a never-succeeding one), and a **consecutive-429 batch bail-out** (reached the point of being ticketed, then dropped: the remedy for a rate-limited run is to run it again later, and a batch that fails every member already reports that). **The spec must not oversell "try again later":** the translation endpoint 429'd on a session's *first* request and after a 4-minute cooldown while native tracks succeeded in the same minute — it is a near-zero standing allowance, not a refilling quota, so the message may say a later run *may* succeed and nothing stronger.

- [Non-speech artifacts in manually-authored subtitle bodies](ytdlp-sab.10): **Four classes, not the three the ticket named, and its framing was wrong on two counts** — credits are 2 of 5 manual files and appear at *both* ends (one track's credit is its final cue), and speaker-change notation is **not** manual-only (`>>` ×17 is the auto costume for manual's `- ` ×51). The fourth, decisive class the ticket missed: **transcriber annotations on speech** (`[Caplin?]`, `[This is a perfect time to get some work done.]`) — brackets mean *opposite* things in the two kinds (`[music]` is noise on auto, content on manual), so that rule can never be uniform; a uniform strip deletes real speech. Dispositions: **credits dropped silently** (manual only, pattern `Transcriber|Reviewer|Translator|Subtitles by|Captions by|Amara` applied *only* to the first and last cue — the position guard is what makes it safe; the seven-key frontmatter stays closed, no `transcriber` key); **speaker notation deleted** (both kinds, token-level — the marker only means something beside a line break, which prose dissolves); **sound events stripped** (both kinds, per-kind notation, **token-level and shape-guarded**: enclosed text ≤4 words with no `.`/`?`/`!`, matched within one cue only — the corpus supports a blunt rule but the guard makes it *fail safe*, leaving an unrecognised long parenthetical visible in the prose rather than silently deleting speech); **annotations kept verbatim**, brackets and all. **HTML entity decoding folded in** rather than ticketed — `>>` is `>>` on disk, so it is a precondition, not a cosmetic. **Pipeline order (refines ytdlp-sab.7's `load → classify → clean`):** `load → classify → strip tags → decode entities → strip artifacts → dedup (auto only) → paragraph`; three edges are forced — classify reads *raw* cue text, decoding must follow tag-stripping or a decoded `<` gets eaten, and stripping must precede dedup because `getOverlapSize` has no minimum `k` and repeated boilerplate is exactly what it mis-fires on. A cue emptied by stripping is dropped (76 of 1504 manual lines). **New standing constraint, recorded in Notes: no LLM in the final application** — it rules out runtime semantic classification and is why the sound-event rule needs a syntactic guard.

## Not yet specified

_Nothing. Every remaining question is a live ticket: the last three fog patches graduated when [Playlist and channel handling](ytdlp-sab.4) closed._

## Out of scope

- **Node-manager configuration on this workstation.** Diagnosed during charting: `fnm use system` pointed the fnm multishell junction at a nonexistent sentinel (`Z:\_fnm_\Nothing\Should\Be\Here\installation`) that stayed on PATH, so `yt-dlp` — being Python and walking PATH — died with `WinError 4392`. Fixed at source by changing the profile to `fnm use default`; verified `yt-dlp` then exits 0 with no PATH sanitization. Machine config sits past this map's destination.
- **Non-YouTube sources.**
- **Chunking or embedding transcripts for RAG.**
- **Summarization** — requires an agent, so it is not a human-reproducible workflow, which is the point of this tool.

title: Tune the paragraph-break threshold
description:
## Question

What fixed pause threshold (and word cap, if any) produces readable paragraphs from YouTube auto-generated captions?

The current cleaner breaks a paragraph when the gap between cues exceeds **2.0s**. In practice this almost never fires on auto-captions — they are near-continuous — so the output is one undifferentiated wall of text. Starting point for tuning is **0.8s**.

Resolve by experiment, not by argument: run the cleaner over 2-3 of the existing `.vtt` files at several gap values, show the user real samples side by side, and let them pick. A **fixed time constant** is the deliverable — no runtime heuristics that would require an agent.

Decide also whether a word cap (break after ~N words regardless of timing) is needed as a backstop, or whether a tuned gap alone is sufficient.

**Answer must state:** the chosen constant(s), and whether they are hard-coded or exposed as CLI flags.
close_reason: Resolved: break at next sentence end past 100 words, hard-coded. Cue-pause thresholds proven unusable (gaps are exactly 0.000s in all 8 files).

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
## Answer

**Rule: break at the next sentence end once the paragraph has reached 100 words. Timing is not used at all.**

```js
const PARAGRAPH_MIN_WORDS = 100;
```

**Hard-coded**, not a CLI flag. The constant proved stable across every speaker tested, so there is nothing for a user to tune, and no flag to document, validate or support.

### The ticket's premise was falsified

The ticket asked for a tuned *pause threshold*, starting at 0.8s. No cue-level pause threshold can ever work: measured across all 8 `.vtt` files in the repo, the gap between consecutive cues is **exactly 0.000s**. YouTube's auto-caption cues are wall-to-wall contiguous by construction (rolling-window captions re-emit the previous line, so each cue starts precisely where the last ended).

Corroborating evidence from production: **every existing `_cleaned.txt` in this repo contains zero blank lines.** The shipped 2.0s rule has never fired once. 0.8s would have been equally dead.

### Why punctuation, not word-level timing

Word-level timings *do* exist (the inline `<00:00:02.560>` markers) and were evaluated. They are speaker-dependent and unreliable:

| Candidate | paragraphs (3 videos) | mean words | longest paragraph |
|---|---|---|---|
| Current (2.0s cue pause) | 1 / 1 / 1 | 2486 / 2258 / 7214 | — one wall of text |
| Word pause >= 1.0s | 15 / 19 / 125 | 166 / 119 / 58 | **696** |
| **Sentence end + 100 words** | **22 / 21 / 64** | **113 / 108 / 113** | **141 / 141 / 160** |
| Sentence end + 60 words | 36 / 33 / 102 | 69 / 68 / 71 | 97 / 103 / 142 |
| Sentence end + 150 words | 16 / 14 / 45 | 155 / 161 / 160 | 178 / 172 / 216 |
| Hybrid (40 words or 0.8s) | 54 / 49 / 169 | 46 / 46 / 43 | 73 / 68 / 123 |

The same timing threshold yields 15, 19 and 125 breaks on three videos, and still leaves 696-word walls. Sentence length, by contrast, is **15.5–19.2 words in all 8 files** — the most stable quantity in the data.

**The punctuation is YouTube's, not ours.** The raw VTT payload is `Skills,<c> skills,</c><c> skills.</c><c> Folks,</c>` — YouTube's ASR emits capitalisation and sentence punctuation. `clean-transcript.js` never inserts a period.

This **inverts the ticket's framing**: the word cap, offered as an optional backstop to a tuned gap, is the primary signal, and timing is dropped entirely. The constraint the ticket actually cared about — a fixed constant, no runtime heuristics needing an agent — is fully honoured.

**Bonus: this transfers to manually-authored subtitles unchanged.** Human-written subs are punctuated by construction but are *not* rolling-window, so a timing rule would have needed a second variant for them. A punctuation-gated word cap needs none.

### Detection rule

A word ends a sentence when it matches `/[.!?]["')\]]?$/`. This false-fires on abbreviations (`etc.`, `Dr.`), which can only end a paragraph slightly early, and only once past the 100-word gate — bounded, and the measured maxima (~1.4x target) confirm it is not pathological. Not worth an abbreviation list.

### Implementation note for the spec

The paragraph splitter needs word-level tokens, but `clean-transcript.js`'s dedup (`getOverlapSize`) discards timings. The prototype ports that dedup onto `{word, onset}` tokens and **verifies the result is identical to `processTranscript` on all 8 files**. Since the chosen rule needs no timings, the implementer may keep plain strings — but the verified parser is on the branch either way.

Also found: `clean-transcript.js` runs its CLI block at module scope, so merely importing it writes a file. The spec must require an entry guard.

### Prototype

Branch `prototype/paragraph-rules` (commit `702d396`) — `.scratch/para/`:
- `words-parse.mjs` — dedup ported onto timed tokens
- `verify.mjs` — proves it matches `processTranscript` on all 8 files
- `rules.mjs`, `build.mjs` — the six candidates
- `paragraph-rules.prototype.html` — the side-by-side the user picked from
