title: Non-speech artifacts in manually-authored subtitle bodies
description:
## Question

What does the cleaner do with the **non-speech artifacts** that manual subtitle bodies carry and auto
tracks do not?

Surfaced while resolving *Dedup safety on manually-authored subtitles* (ytdlp-sab.7) — this was the
project's first look inside a manual VTT body, and none of these are handled. The cleaner's only
filters are the header skip list (`WEBVTT`, `Kind:`, `Language:`, bare digits) and `<...>` tag
stripping, so every artifact below lands in the prose verbatim. Measured across the 5 manual samples
on `prototype/dedup-safety`:

**1. Translator credit cues** — 1 of 5 files. `rNxC16mlO60` cue 0 is a real cue with a real
timestamp:

```
00:00:00.000 --> 00:00:07.000
Transcriber: isabella hilário
Reviewer: Emma Gon
```

`Transcriber:` matches no skip-list entry and sits *after* the first timestamp, so it becomes
`cues[0]`. Verified: the transcript body currently **opens** with
`Transcriber: isabella hilário Reviewer: Emma Gon`. Every community-captioned TED talk carries this.
*Markdown output and filename contract* (ytdlp-sab.2) settled the body as plain prose with no H1 and
no timestamps; it is silent on credits.

**2. Dialogue dashes** — 51 cues in `DxL2HoqLbyA`, 0 in all 8 auto files. A leading `- ` is
speaker-change notation. With dedup now off on manual tracks the echo survives too, so the body reads
`- Warmth. - Warmth, light.` — speaker notation inside prose that has no speakers. Verified: that
transcript now opens `- This is a video about…`.

**3. Sound events, in two different notations.** Manual tracks use **parenthesised and capitalised**:
`(Laughter)` ×26 and ×40, `(Applause)`, `(Sigh)`, `(Audience)`. Auto tracks use **bracketed and
lowercase**: `[music]`, `[laughter]`, `[snorts]`. Both classes reach the body untouched today, and any
rule has to cover both notations — this one is **not** manual-only.

Decide: whether each class is stripped, kept, or normalised; whether credit cues are dropped silently
or the transcriber is surfaced somewhere (note the seven-key frontmatter is settled and has no slot,
so "surface it" means reopening a settled contract, or not doing it); whether dialogue dashes are
deleted, or kept as a signal that this transcript has multiple speakers; and whether sound events are
prose-worthy context or noise. Watch for a filter that is too eager — a sentence can legitimately
begin with a parenthesis, and a hyphen can open a line of verse.

**Answer must state:** the disposition of each of the three classes, whether the rule is
track-kind-dependent or uniform, and the order it runs in relative to the `load → classify → clean`
pipeline settled in ytdlp-sab.7.
close_reason: Four artifact classes settled: credits dropped silently (manual, position-guarded), speaker notation deleted (both kinds), sound events stripped token-level with a shape guard (both kinds, per-kind notation), transcriber annotations kept verbatim. Entity decoding folded in. Pipeline: load, classify, strip tags, decode entities, strip artifacts, dedup auto-only, paragraph.

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
## Resolution

**Four classes, not three.** The ticket's framing was corrected by re-measuring the corpus (5 manual
VTTs / 1504 cues on `prototype/dedup-safety`, 8 auto VTTs / 10,869 cues at the repo root). Sorting by
what an artifact *encodes* rather than by its punctuation:

| Class | manual notation | auto notation |
|---|---|---|
| Provenance credits | `Transcriber:` / `Reviewer:` (first cue), `Subtitles by the Amara.org community` (last cue) | none |
| Speaker change | `- ` ×51, 1 file | `>>` ×17, 3 files |
| Sound events | `(Laughter)` ×66, `(Applause)` ×8, `(Cheers and applause)` ×2, `(Sigh)`, `(Audience)` | `[snorts]` ×27, `[music]` ×4, `[laughter]` ×4, `[clears throat]` ×3 |
| Transcriber annotations on speech | `[Caplin?]`, `[This is a perfect time to get some work done.] [Nope!]` | none |

Two corrections to the ticket body: **credits are 2 of 5 files, not 1 of 5, and not head-only** (one
track carries the credit as its *final* cue at 00:03:35, so a "drop `cues[0]`" rule catches neither
notation); and **speaker-change notation is not manual-only** — `>>` is the auto costume for `- `.

The fourth class is the decisive one and the ticket did not see it. **Brackets mean opposite things
in the two track kinds**: `[music]` in an auto track is noise, `[Caplin?]` (an uncertain proper name)
and `[This is a perfect time to get some work done.]` (on-screen text) in a manual track are content.
A uniform bracket strip deletes real speech. That is settled by evidence, not preference.

Also measured: across all 1504 manual cues **every** parenthetical is a sound event — there are no
legitimate parenthetical asides in the corpus. And `>` ×34 / `&` ×3 reach the body undecoded
in both track kinds; the cleaner never decodes entities. Brackets can open in one cue and close in
the next (`[This is a perfect time` / `to get some work done.]`).

### Disposition

**1. Provenance credits — dropped silently. Manual only.** Drop the whole cue when it is the first
or last cue of a manual track and any of its lines matches, case-insensitively,
`^\s*(Transcriber|Reviewer|Translator|Subtitles by|Captions by|Amara)\b`. The position guard is what
makes the pattern safe: "subtitles by…" is a phrase a speaker could plausibly utter mid-talk, but as
the terminal cue of a file it cannot be anything else. **Not surfaced anywhere** — the seven-key
frontmatter stays closed. These captioners worked for viewers, not for a Markdown file, and the
transcript already carries `url`; attribution lives at the source. Rejected: an eighth optional
`transcriber` key (reopens a settled contract for a field empty in 3 of 5 manual tracks and all auto
tracks), and keeping the credit in the body (the status quo, which opens one transcript with
`Transcriber: isabella hilário Reviewer: Emma Gon`).

**2. Speaker-change notation — deleted, both notations, token-level.** On manual, a leading `- ` at
the start of a cue line; on auto, a leading `>>` plus following whitespace. The cue survives minus the
marker. The marker is only meaningful next to a *line break*, which prose has already dissolved: once
cues merge into a 100-word paragraph a bare `- ` mid-sentence marks nothing a reader can use.
Rejected: normalising both to one output form, and recording "this transcript had multiple speakers"
(another frontmatter reopening for a fact nobody asked for).

**3. Sound events — stripped, both notations, token-level, shape-guarded.** Remove a `(…)` token on
a manual track and a `[…]` token on an auto track when the enclosed text is **≤4 words and contains
no `.`, `?` or `!`**. Matching is within a single cue's text only — an unclosed bracket or paren is
left alone, which is what keeps the cross-cue `[This is a perfect time` case intact.

The shape guard is the deliberate cost. The corpus supports a blunt rule (on manual, 100% of
parentheticals are sound events), but 5 manual files is a thin basis for betting that no speaker ever
gets a parenthetical aside, and the failure mode of that bet is speech deleted silently with nothing
in the output to hint at it. The guard is one condition and makes the rule **fail safe**: an
unrecognised long parenthetical stays in the prose where it can be seen. Rejected: a curated
vocabulary (`laughter|applause|music|…`) — it needs curating forever against ASR's open vocabulary,
`[snorts]` was on nobody's list, and under the no-LLM constraint there is no fallback that could ever
catch an unlisted token.

`(Laughter)` is not spoken content, it is stage direction, and it survives into the paragraph
mid-sentence where it reads as an interruption. Rejected: keeping manual's events and stripping
auto's — defensible, but it makes the same reader-facing artifact appear or vanish according to who
captioned the video, which is exactly the track-kind leakage the `subtitles` frontmatter key exists to
disclose.

**4. Transcriber annotations — kept verbatim, brackets and all.** No rule; the bracket rule simply
does not apply to manual tracks. The brackets *are* the meaning: unwrapping turns `Matt [Caplin?],`
into `Matt Caplin?,` — a question mark that now reads as the speaker's, not the transcriber's — and
unwrapping would require matching an opener to a closer across cues, which keeping verbatim does not.

**5. HTML entities — decoded, uniform across both kinds.** Folded in from the ticket's discussion
rather than ticketed separately: it is one line of the pipeline order this ticket had to state anyway,
and it has no trade-off in it. It is not cosmetic here — `>>` is `>>` on disk, so the decode is
a *precondition* of the speaker-notation rule, and one rule then covers both.

### Track-kind dependence

| Class | Dependence |
|---|---|
| Credits | **manual only** |
| Speaker change | **both**, different notation per kind |
| Sound events | **both**, different notation per kind — and the same notation (`[…]`) means opposite things, so this rule can never be uniform |
| Annotations | **manual only** (the consequence of the row above) |
| Entity decode | **uniform** |

### Pipeline order

`load → classify → strip tags → decode entities → strip artifacts → dedup (auto only) → paragraph`

Refines the `load → classify → clean` settled in ytdlp-sab.7 by expanding `clean`. Three of the edges
are forced, not stylistic:

- **classify before everything**: the `<c>` word-timing rule reads *raw* cue text, and every artifact
rule below branches on the answer. This is the classifier's third consumer (frontmatter key, dedup
skip, now artifact notation).
- **decode entities after `<…>` tag stripping**: decoding first would turn a `<` into a `<` that
tag-stripping then eats along with everything up to the next `>`.
- **strip artifacts before dedup**: `getOverlapSize` has no minimum `k` — that is the whole finding of
ytdlp-sab.7 — so feeding it repeated boilerplate like `>>` and `[laughter]` (which recurs 3× in one
file) hands it exactly the repetition it mis-fires on. Every artifact is destined for deletion anyway,
so matching on it can only produce noise; stripping first leaves dedup seeing only prose, which is what
its heuristic was tuned against.

**Cue-level consequence of token-level removal.** Disposition is token-level because speech shares the
line with the token — `(Audience) Good.` and `Thank you. (Applause)`. After removal: collapse runs of
whitespace, trim, and **drop the cue entirely if nothing but whitespace remains** (76 of 1504 manual
lines are sound-event-only). A dropped cue contributes no words, so paragraph accumulation simply skips
it; `PARAGRAPH_MIN_WORDS` is unaffected.

### Constraint recorded on the map

**No LLM in the final application** — raised during this ticket, written into the map's Notes as a
standing constraint for the whole effort. Every rule above is regex, position, or counting. It rules
out runtime semantic classification of a token, and it is why rule 3 needs a syntactic guard: with no
semantic judgement available, the shape test is the only thing standing between the strip rule and
real speech.

### Measured, not ticketed

Auto-track parentheticals: **zero** across 10,869 cues, and zero leading `- `. Manual `>>`: zero. The
notations do not cross kinds, so no rule needs to handle the crossed case.

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
## Addendum: position of the Amara credit, verified; and one output consequence the implementer will misread

**The position guard holds.** The credit rule's safety argument rests on `Subtitles by the Amara.org community` being the *terminal* cue of `8nHBGFKLHZQ`, which the resolution asserted from a windowed read. Verified directly: it is the last cue in the file (`00:03:35.000 --> 00:03:38.000`, nothing after it). A first-or-last-cue guard catches both credit notations in the corpus.

**The speaker echo survives as prose — this is intended.** Deleting `- ` turns `- Warmth. - Warmth, light.` into `Warmth. Warmth, light.` Nothing in the output marks it as a two-speaker exchange, so it reads as an accidental duplication. It is not: dedup is *off* on manual tracks by ytdlp-sab.7, because on that corpus dedup scored 0 true positives against 13 false positives, deleting real speech in every case. An implementer who sees this in output and "fixes" it by re-enabling dedup on manual tracks reinstates exactly the corruption that ticket measured. The hand-off should say so where it will be read before the fix is attempted.

title: Markdown output and filename contract
description:
## Question

What exactly does a transcript file look like, and what is it called?

**Filename.** Kebab-case of the video title. The edge cases are real and present in this repo already: an en-dash, a title beginning with `--`, and the general problem of emoji, `|`, `:`, `?`, `/`, and non-ASCII characters. Decide the slug algorithm, whether there is a length cap, and what happens on **collision** (two videos, one title).

**Body.** YAML frontmatter carrying `title`, `url`, `duration`, `fetched`, `channel`, `upload_date`, `subtitles` (`manual` | `auto`), followed by the cleaned transcript. Decide whether the title is repeated as an H1, whether paragraphs are plain or carry timestamps, and anything else the body needs to be useful as agent input.

**Re-runs.** Requesting a video that already has a transcript: overwrite, skip, or error?

**Answer must state:** the slug algorithm precisely enough to implement, the exact frontmatter key set and value formats, the body layout, and the re-run policy.
close_reason: Transcript file contract settled: slug algorithm + 120-char cap + video-id fallback, seven-key frontmatter with explicit value formats, plain-prose body with no H1 or timestamps, and URL-based identity with silent overwrite on re-run.

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
## Answer: the transcript file contract

### Filename

One file per video in flat `transcripts/`, extension `.md`.

**Slug algorithm**, applied to the video title, in order:

1. Unicode-normalise NFKD and strip combining marks (diacritics folded to ASCII).
2. Lowercase.
3. **Delete** apostrophes and quote marks (`'`, `’`, `"`, `“`, `”`) outright — no separator. `Don't` → `dont`, not `don-t`.
4. Replace every remaining run of characters outside `[a-z0-9]` with a single `-`.
5. Trim leading and trailing `-`.

No special cases. Step 5 is what disposes of the `--` prefix and the leading `/` in `/wayfinder:` without special-casing either. `&` falls out as a separator (`Build & Deploy` → `build-deploy`); dots are separators too, so `v1.2` → `v1-2` and `INTENT.MD` → `intent-md`.

**Length cap: 120 characters**, truncated at the last `-` boundary at or before 120, trailing `-` trimmed. The full title is never lost — it is in the frontmatter.

**Empty slug** (title is entirely non-Latin — Greek, Japanese, Cyrillic — or pure emoji/punctuation): fall back to the **video id** as the filename, e.g. `o3CX_Y59_74.md`. No transliteration dependency.

**Verified test vector** — the eight videos already in this repo, with live yt-dlp titles:

| title | slug |
|---|---|
| How to Fine-Tune any AI Model Locally (FULL Tutorial) | `how-to-fine-tune-any-ai-model-locally-full-tutorial` |
| /wayfinder: Nothing is too big to plan anymore | `wayfinder-nothing-is-too-big-to-plan-anymore` |
| New Skills! v1.2 brings /wait-what, /writing-for-agents, and fixes /grill-me | `new-skills-v1-2-brings-wait-what-writing-for-agents-and-fixes-grill-me` |
| The Best LOCAL Agentic Coding Workflow (Complete Guide) | `the-best-local-agentic-coding-workflow-complete-guide` |
| Claude Codes New INTENT.MD, What is It? | `claude-codes-new-intent-md-what-is-it` |
| mattpocock/skills: A complete AI Coding workflow, end-to-end | `mattpocock-skills-a-complete-ai-coding-workflow-end-to-end` |
| Don't waste time on specs: /prototype instead | `dont-waste-time-on-specs-prototype-instead` |
| OpenAI Codex Crash Course – Build & Deploy Apps with Autonomous AI | `openai-codex-crash-course-build-deploy-apps-with-autonomous-ai` |

These eight are the implementer's test cases: they cover a leading `/`, an en-dash, a `&`, an apostrophe, dots inside a version number and inside `INTENT.MD`, parentheses, `!`, `?`, and commas.

### Frontmatter

Exactly seven keys, in this order:

```yaml
---
title: "OpenAI Codex Crash Course – Build & Deploy Apps with Autonomous AI"
url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o3CX_Y59_74
channel: "freeCodeCamp.org"
duration: "41:18"
upload_date: 2026-09-10
fetched: 2026-09-16T14:03:05Z
subtitles: auto
---
```

Value formats, all deliberate:

- **`title`** and **`channel`**: **always** double-quoted, with `\` and `"` escaped. Unconditional, not quote-when-needed. Three of the eight titles contain a `:` and one begins with `/`; `title: /wayfinder: Nothing is too big...` is invalid YAML. A conditional rule is one an implementer gets subtly wrong.
- **`url`**: normalised to `https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=<id>` regardless of input form (`youtu.be/`, `/shorts/`, bare id, `?si=`/`&t=` junk). One shape on disk, one regex to read it back. Safe bare.
- **`duration`**: **always double-quoted** — `duration: 41:18` unquoted is *not a string*; YAML 1.1 parsers read colon-separated digits as a sexagesimal integer and yield `2478`, and parsers disagree with each other about it. Format is `M:SS`, widening to `H:MM:SS` only once the video passes an hour. No zero-padding on the leading unit, matching how YouTube itself displays durations.
- **`upload_date`**: reformatted from yt-dlp's native `20260910` to `2026-09-10`. A bare `20260910` is a number-shaped string that YAML parsers and humans both misread.
- **`fetched`**: full ISO-8601 **UTC** instant, `Z`-suffixed. A date alone loses same-day re-fetches, and freshness is the whole point of the field.
- **`subtitles`**: `manual` or `auto`, bare.

No `video_id` key — `url` carries it.

### Body

Immediately after the closing `---`: the cleaned transcript as plain prose paragraphs separated by blank lines. **No H1** (the title is in the frontmatter; repeating it is redundant for the agent that consumes this) and **no per-paragraph timestamps** (noise in prose, and the paragraphing decision already established that this pipeline's timing data is unusable). Paragraphs break per `PARAGRAPH_MIN_WORDS = 100` at the next sentence end.

### Identity and re-runs

**Identity is the frontmatter `url`, never the filename.** A transcript for video X exists **iff** some file in `transcripts/` has a frontmatter `url` whose video id is X.

This matters because the slug alone cannot distinguish "re-fetch of the same video" from "different video that happens to share a title". The scan costs nothing new — the catalog is derived by reading every transcript's frontmatter anyway.

- **Re-run of the same video** → **overwrite in place, silently**, and bump `fetched`. A transcript is derived data; re-fetching is precisely how you pick up improved auto-captions.
- **Different video, same slug** → the *second* file gains a video-id suffix: `same-title-<videoid>.md`. Only the loser of the collision is uglified; the common case stays clean.

**This is the definition ticket _Playlist and channel handling_ needs for "already fetched":** a catalog/frontmatter `url` lookup, not a filename match.

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
## Addendum: the slug rule drops non-Latin letters silently

The empty-slug fallback above covers a title that slugifies to **nothing**. Reviewing the algorithm against mixed-script and Latin-extended titles exposed a worse case it does *not* cover.

**Mixed script.** `Νέα Skills! v1.2 για agents` → the Greek letters carry no combining marks, so NFKD leaves them intact, and step 4 turns each run into a separator. Result: `skills-v1-2`. Non-empty, so the video-id fallback never fires — and the filename has silently swallowed most of the title while looking perfectly plausible. That is strictly worse than `o3CX_Y59_74.md`, which at least announces that it gave up.

**Latin-extended.** The same mechanism, one character at a time: `Søren` → `s-ren`, `Paweł` → `pawe-`, `Straße` → `stra-e`. No combining mark to strip, so a letter becomes punctuation.

### Refinement

Two additions, both inside the existing algorithm — nothing else about the contract changes:

1. **Between steps 2 and 3, transliterate the Latin letters NFKD does not decompose**, via a small fixed table: `ø→o`, `ł→l`, `đ→d`, `ß→ss`, `æ→ae`, `œ→oe`, `þ→th`, `ð→d`. This fixes the Latin-extended case properly rather than giving up on it: `soren`, `pawel`, `strasse`.

2. **After step 5, compute a retention ratio**: alphanumeric characters in the slug, divided by Unicode letters-plus-digits in the original title. **If retention is below 50%, discard the slug and use the video id as the filename.**

Rule 2 subsumes the empty-slug case (retention 0%), so it replaces that clause rather than sitting beside it. Under it, `Νέα Skills! v1.2 για agents` retains roughly 30% and correctly falls back to the id; all eight titles in the verified test vector retain 100% and are unaffected.

Rationale: a filename is a convenience, and a *misleading* convenience is worth less than an honest video id. The frontmatter `title` and the catalog both carry the real title regardless, and identity rests on the frontmatter `url`, so a fallback filename costs nothing functional.

title: Catalog contents and rebuild semantics
description:
## Question

What is in the catalog, and how is it rebuilt?

A Markdown file, **derived** from the frontmatter of the files in `transcripts/` so it cannot drift from reality.

Decide: where it lives (`transcripts/README.md`, repo root, elsewhere); which columns it carries and in what order; how it sorts; whether it links to each transcript by relative path; and how rebuild is triggered — automatically after every fetch, via an explicit flag on the single entry point, or both.

Constraint from the user: no script calling another script, and no proliferation of scripts. Rebuild is a mode of the one CLI, not a second executable.

**Answer must state:** the catalog's path, its exact column set, sort order, and the rebuild trigger.
close_reason: Catalog is transcripts/README.md; five derived columns; upload_date desc; rebuild both automatic and via the yt-transcript catalog subcommand, always a full rescan.

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
## Answer

**Path:** `transcripts/README.md`. It is the folder's front door, renders automatically when the directory is opened, and sits next to what it is derived from. The rebuild scans the directory containing its own output, so the scan rule is **"any `.md` with parseable frontmatter is a transcript"** — the README has none and is excluded as a side effect, with no filename special-case.

**Columns** (exact set, exact order):

| Column | Source | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Title | `title` | Hyperlinked to the transcript's relative path |
| Channel | `channel` | |
| Duration | `duration` | Rendered as stored |
| Uploaded | `upload_date` | `YYYY-MM-DD` |
| Subtitles | `subtitles` | `manual` or `auto` |

Two frontmatter keys are deliberately **not** surfaced: `url` (the Title already links onward into the transcript, and the YouTube URL is one step further in, in the file's own frontmatter) and `fetched` (provenance, not something you browse by — and including it would churn a table row on every re-fetch).

Every column is computable from the seven frontmatter keys plus the file's own path. That is the acceptance test for any future column: if it is not derivable from those, it does not belong in the catalog, because admitting it would either reopen the closed frontmatter contract or reintroduce exactly the drift the catalog exists to prevent.

**Sort:** `upload_date` **descending**, tie-break `title` **ascending**. Both keys are immutable, so a re-fetch never reorders a row. Sorting by `fetched` was rejected for precisely that churn; alphabetical-by-title was rejected because a library of talks reads best newest-first.

**Rebuild trigger: both.** Automatically after every **successful** fetch, and explicitly via `yt-transcript catalog`. Automatic-only goes stale the moment a transcript is deleted or hand-edited outside the tool — which is exactly when an index starts lying. Explicit-only makes the common path two commands.

`catalog` is a **subcommand** on the single entry point, not a flag, and not a second executable. `yt-transcript <url|id>` remains the bare default. The reasoning: rebuild takes no target and does something categorically different from fetching, which is what a verb slot is for; a second mode-flag later would fight the first.

Rebuild is **always a full rescan**, never an incremental append. That is what makes drift structurally impossible rather than merely unlikely.

**Above the table:** an `# Transcripts` H1, then a single line — `N transcripts, regenerated by ` + `yt-transcript catalog` — then the table. The regeneration note is load-bearing: the file is derived, so anyone hand-editing it loses the edit on the next fetch and the file must say so. The count is free and makes an incomplete rebuild visible at a glance.

**Malformed transcript:** a `.md` whose frontmatter is unparseable or missing required keys is **skipped with a warning** naming the file and telling the user to re-download it. Not silent — a transcript vanishing from the index with no signal is the precise failure a derived catalog exists to prevent. Not fatal — one bad file should not cost you the whole catalog.

## Consequences settled here

- **Stub rows are impossible by construction.** The catalog is a pure function of the directory, so it cannot hold a row for a video with no transcript file. This **constrains** the open *No subtitles at all* question: "record a stub in the catalog" is only reachable by writing a real transcript file with real frontmatter. That remains that ticket's call; the constraint is recorded, the fog patch is not resolved.
- **Pipe escaping.** A `|` in a video title would break the Markdown table row, so titles are escaped as `\|` **in the catalog cell only**. The frontmatter and filename contracts are untouched.
- **Empty state.** Zero transcripts yields the H1 and a `0 transcripts` line with no table, rather than an empty table skeleton.

## Deferred, not decided

Whether the catalog records **playlist membership** belongs to *Playlist and channel handling* and was deliberately not settled here. Note for that ticket: any playlist column must pass the derivability test above, which today it fails — playlist provenance is not among the seven frontmatter keys, so recording it means amending the frontmatter contract, not just the catalog.

## No ADR

Path, column set and sort are all cheap to reverse and unsurprising. The rebuild trigger is the expected answer rather than a contested trade-off. None of the three ADR criteria is met.

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
## Amended by Playlist and channel handling (ytdlp-sab.4)

This ticket settled that a rebuild fires automatically **after every successful fetch**. That rule is
now narrowed: after every successful **single-video** fetch, and **once at the end of a batch** — not
once per video, which would make a 200-video playlist run quadratic.

Everything else here stands unchanged: the rebuild is still always a full rescan, still also available
explicitly via `yt-transcript catalog`, and the catalog is still derived wholly from frontmatter.

Accepted consequence: a batch interrupted part-way leaves transcripts on disk that the catalog does not
yet list, until `yt-transcript catalog` is run. Because the catalog is derived and rebuilt by full
rescan, that state can only ever be incomplete, never wrong.

Also decided there, and relevant to this ticket: playlist provenance is **not** recorded, so the seven
frontmatter keys and the five catalog columns are unchanged by playlist support.

title: Playlist and channel handling
description:
## Question

What happens when the user hands `yt-transcript` a playlist or channel URL?

Playlist and channel support is in scope; the single entry point detects a playlist itself rather than delegating to a separate script.

Decide: how a playlist/channel URL is distinguished from a video URL; whether already-fetched videos are skipped (and what "already fetched" means — filename match, or catalog lookup); what happens when one video in a batch fails (abort, continue-and-report, retry); whether there is a cap or rate limit; and whether the catalog records playlist membership at all.

**Answer must state:** the detection rule, the skip rule, the partial-failure policy, and whether playlist provenance is recorded.
close_reason: Resolved: detection is syntactic and video-wins on list=; skip is batch-only keyed on frontmatter url; continue-and-report with a named 429 exception; no provenance recorded.

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
## Resolution

A playlist or channel URL **expands** into a **batch** of fetches. Each fetch is still one video, one
`yt-dlp` invocation; the batch is the only new unit.

### Detection rule — purely syntactic, no network call

Verified: yt-dlp selects its extractor by regex before any network I/O, so URL shape alone decides.

- `watch?v=<id>` (with or without `&si=`/`&t=` junk), `youtu.be/<id>`, `/shorts/<id>`, bare id → **one video**.
- `/playlist?list=<id>` → **batch**.
- `youtube.com/@handle`, `/c/Name`, `/channel/UC…` → **batch**, rewritten to the channel's **Videos tab**.
- `watch?v=<id>&list=<listid>` → **one video**. `list=` is discarded like other trailing junk;
  `--playlist` forces the batch reading.

Two divergences from `yt-dlp` that must be implemented deliberately, not inherited:

1. yt-dlp's default on `watch?v=&list=` is the **opposite** — it takes the whole playlist. We must pass
   `--no-playlist`. A URL carrying `v=` names a video: that is what the user copied from the address bar
   while watching, and the playlist tail is an artifact of how they arrived. Deliberate playlist intent
   has its own URL form; accidental playlist intent costs 200 downloads.
2. A bare `@handle` expands in yt-dlp to **Videos + Shorts + Live** as three sub-playlists (verified on a
   real channel). We rewrite it to the Videos tab. A 45-second Short is not a video you have no time to
   watch, and a livestream's auto-captions are mostly silence. `@handle/shorts` and `@handle/streams`
   are still honoured when named explicitly — the narrowing applies only to the ambiguous bare form.

### Skip rule — expand first, batch only

- **Single video URL: never skipped.** The settled overwrite-always behaviour from *Markdown output and
  filename contract* is untouched. Naming one video is a command; you meant it.
- **Batch: skipped by default.** The URL list is obtained by a flat expansion
  (`--flat-playlist --simulate --print`), normalised to the settled `https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=<id>`
  form, and subtracted from the URLs already present in `transcripts/` frontmatter. Only the remainder is
  fetched, so the skip saves the download, not merely the file write.
- Identity is the frontmatter `url`, never the filename — inherited unchanged.
- The known-URL set comes from the **same full scan of `transcripts/` that the catalog rebuild performs**.
  One scan implementation, two callers.
- `--force` has exactly one meaning: **ignore the skip set**. On a single video URL it is accepted and is
  a silent no-op, so scripts may pass it uniformly. There is no `--no-playlist` counterpart flag.
- Expansion is cheap enough to make this the obvious order: a 50-item playlist costs **2 HTTP requests**,
  200 items costs 7.

### Partial-failure policy — continue, collect, report

- A failed video never stops the batch. Each failure is collected with its reason and printed in a summary
  at the end, naming the video — mirroring the catalog's settled "skipped with a warning naming the file"
  posture. Never silent, never fatal.
- **No general retry layer.** yt-dlp already retries network faults, and our failures are mostly permanent:
  deleted, private, members-only, region-blocked.
- **HTTP 429 is the one named exception**, because it is transient and retrying is the correct response.
  Three attempts, backing off 5s / 15s / 45s, then the video enters the failure summary labelled
  *rate-limited* — distinct from other reasons, because it tells the user to re-run later rather than to
  give up. This is not a hole in the no-retry rule; the rule was reasoned from permanence, and a rate-limit
  response is not permanent.
- **Exit non-zero if any video failed**, so a scripted run cannot quietly under-deliver.
- **Success is exit code 0 AND a non-empty subtitle file on disk.** Exit code alone is insufficient:
  requesting a subtitle language that does not exist exits **0 with no error line and no file** (verified).
  A file that arrives but cleans to nothing is a cleaner bug — loud and separate, not a fetch failure.
- Because we expand ourselves and invoke yt-dlp once per video, exit codes are per-video and unambiguous.
  yt-dlp's own inability to distinguish "all failed" from "some failed" via exit code never reaches us.

### Batch-level failure, as distinct from failure within a batch

- **Expansion failure is a hard error**: private playlist, deleted channel, mistyped handle. No batch
  starts, non-zero exit, no catalog rebuild.
- **Zero videos returned is not an error** — reports `0 videos`, exits 0.
- **A batch where every video is already fetched is a success** — reports
  `47 videos, 47 already fetched, nothing to do`, exits 0.
- The line is whether we failed to *learn what the URL names*, versus learning it names nothing new.

### Rate limiting — a delay, not a cap

- **No cap on batch size.** Any number would defend an unquantified threshold: it would block legitimate
  use without guaranteeing safety.
- **A fixed one-second delay between fetches in batch mode**, implemented by our own batch loop; the
  single-video path is untouched. This is deliberately *not* a yt-dlp flag: because we expand ourselves
  and spawn yt-dlp once per video, `--sleep-requests` (sleeps between requests *during extraction*) and
  `--sleep-interval` / `--sleep-subtitles` (sleep *before* a download) all act **inside** a single
  invocation and cannot space one spawn from the next. Only the caller can do that. (Implementer note,
  not a decision: `--sleep-requests` was purpose-built for exactly this throttling problem — yt-dlp #106
  — so it remains the first lever to reach for if one-second spacing proves insufficient.)
- The risk is specific to us, not hypothetical: yt-dlp's sleep flags all **default to off**, and yt-dlp
  issue **#13831** is an open report of **429s on auto-generated subtitle requests** — the exact call a
  batch makes hundreds of times. A maintainer records that an earlier fix held only "for a while" before
  YouTube tightened further, and no workaround is reliable. No one cites a volume threshold, which is
  precisely why a numeric cap would be theatre and a one-second sleep is the only lever with evidence
  behind it.

### Playlist provenance — not recorded

A transcript does not remember the playlist it arrived via. The frontmatter stays **exactly seven keys**,
and the catalog gains no column. Three reasons: it would break a settled contract; playlist membership is
not a property of the video (one video sits in many playlists, and membership changes after the fetch, so
the field would rot); and `channel` already answers the question people actually ask. **The playlist is how
you found the video, not what the video is.**

`playlist_id` / `playlist_title` / `playlist_index` / `playlist_uploader` are all reliably available from
yt-dlp and are deliberately discarded. (`playlist_count` is `NA` on channel tabs, so a progress total on a
channel must come from our own expansion, not from that field.)

### Catalog rebuild — amends *Catalog contents and rebuild semantics*

That ticket settled "rebuild fires automatically after every successful fetch." **This narrows it:** after
every successful *single-video* fetch, and **once at the end of a batch** — not once per video, which would
make a 200-video run quadratic.

**Accepted consequence:** a batch interrupted by `Ctrl-C` or a crash leaves transcripts on disk that the
catalog does not list, until someone runs `yt-transcript catalog`. The catalog remains derived and a full
rescan, so the remedy is always one command and can never produce a wrong result — only a briefly
incomplete one.

### Ordering and output

- Fetches run in **playlist order as yt-dlp returns it**: the creator's intended order, stable across runs,
  so an interrupted batch resumes predictably. Fetch order does not affect the catalog, whose sort is
  settled independently as `upload_date` descending.
- A batch prints an **expansion line** up front (total / already fetched / to fetch), **one line per video**
  as it completes (index, count, title, and whether manual or auto subtitles were used), and the **failure
  summary** at the end.
- The single-video path prints that same per-video line. A batch is a fetch repeated, so it gets no display
  language of its own; `1/1` reads fine.

### CLI surface after this ticket

```
yt-transcript <video-url|id>          one fetch, overwrites
yt-transcript <playlist-url>          batch, skips already-fetched
yt-transcript <channel-url>           batch over the Videos tab
yt-transcript catalog                 full rescan (settled previously)
  --playlist                          force the batch reading of watch?v=...&list=...
  --force                             ignore the skip set (no-op on a single video)
```

### Glossary

`CONTEXT.md` gained **Batch** and **Expand**, and **Fetch** was tightened to exactly one video —
a playlist is many fetches, never one large one.

### Deliberately not decided here

**What the CLI does when a video has no captions at all** in the requested language. This ticket settles
only how a fetch *detects* that condition so a batch can report it; the policy — hard error, or fall back to
another language — graduates to its own ticket.

Evidence for every yt-dlp behavioural claim above: `archive/research/yt-dlp-playlist-and-channel-urls.md`.

title: yt-dlp-ejs and pure-JS viability
description:
## Question

Is `yt-dlp-ejs` usable in our case, and is a pure-JavaScript transcript pipeline durable enough to replace the `yt-dlp` binary?

Running `yt-dlp` today emits a deprecation warning: no supported JavaScript runtime found, only Deno enabled by default, "YouTube extraction without a JS runtime has been deprecated". Two things to establish:

1. **yt-dlp-ejs** (https://github.com/yt-dlp/ejs) — what it is, whether Node can serve as the runtime instead of Deno and with what `--js-runtimes` syntax, whether it must be installed separately, whether the warning affects **subtitle downloads** specifically or only media format extraction, and whether there is a deadline after which extraction breaks.
2. **Pure-JS alternatives** — whether any maintained npm package reliably fetches auto-generated captions, metadata, and playlists against current YouTube bot-detection, with evidence from recent issues rather than marketing copy.

The user's preference rule is settled: **robustness wins.** Pure-JS is adopted only if it is durable, not merely possible. The expected outcome is confirmation that spawning `yt-dlp` is correct, plus a concrete answer on whether to pass `--js-runtimes` to silence/avoid the deprecation.

**Answer must state:** whether ejs is usable here, whether the warning matters for subtitles, and the final fetching architecture.
close_reason: Resolved: spawn yt-dlp binary; pure-JS not durable; --js-runtimes node as insurance. Subtitle immunity verified live (byte-identical output).

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
## Answer

**Keep spawning the `yt-dlp` binary. Pure-JS is not durable. `yt-dlp-ejs` is not needed for our case, but pass `--js-runtimes node` as cheap insurance.**

### Is ejs usable here?

`yt-dlp-ejs` is a **challenge-solver script package, not a runtime**. It solves YouTube's n/signature and BotGuard-style JS challenges inside a separate JS engine that yt-dlp invokes. Node **is** officially supported via `--js-runtimes node` (minimum v22; this machine runs v24), but it is second-tier — Deno is the only first-class default and silently wins if both are installed, so forcing Node where Deno also exists needs `--no-js-runtimes --js-runtimes node`. The ejs component ships bundled in official yt-dlp executables.

### Does the warning affect subtitles? — **Verified live: no.**

The research flagged this as unresolved, inferring from yt-dlp's PO Token Guide (which lists "Subs" as its own PO-Token-gated case) that subtitle fetches might be affected. Reproduced directly instead, on this machine, against `gaDdrDdczO4`:

| Run | Command | Result |
|---|---|---|
| A | `--write-auto-sub --sub-lang en --skip-download` | `gaDdrDdczO4.en.vtt` — **122,555 bytes** |
| B | `--js-runtimes node --write-auto-sub --sub-lang en --skip-download` | `gaDdrDdczO4.en.vtt` — **122,555 bytes** |

Identical size, and identical to the copy already in the repo. The deprecation warning is **cosmetic for our use case today**: auto-caption downloads do not currently need a JS runtime. `--js-runtimes node` is accepted without error and suppresses the warning.

No formal deadline for a hard break has been announced — only an open-ended "expected to worsen" statement. Hard failures already occur today for logged-in and age-gated content, neither of which we touch.

### Pure-JS alternatives — not viable

- `ytdl-core`: unmaintained since 2023.
- `@distube/ytdl-core`: repository archived; its own README redirects users to `youtubei.js`.
- `youtubei.js`: the only actively maintained full-featured candidate, but rides the same YouTube-chasing treadmill as yt-dlp, with recent bot-detection/403 issues, and does not solve PoToken generation itself.
- Transcript-only scrapers (`youtube-transcript`, `youtube-captions-scraper`): no PoToken handling, documented IP-banning failures by design.

Replacing yt-dlp with any of these trades a tool maintained specifically to survive YouTube's countermeasures for one that is not. Against the settled preference rule — robustness wins — that trade fails.

### Architecture, settled

Node CLI spawns the `yt-dlp` binary as a child process. Preflight-check for `yt-dlp` on PATH and fail with a clear, actionable message if absent. Pass `--js-runtimes node` on every invocation: it costs nothing, silences the deprecation warning, and means the pipeline keeps working on the day subtitles *do* start requiring a runtime.

### Caveats carried forward

The verification above is a single video at a single point in time. If auto-captions ever come back empty or truncated, `--js-runtimes node` is already in place, and the next thing to check is PO Token requirements for the `web` client.

Full research report with citations: `docs/research/yt-dlp-js-runtime-and-pure-js-paths.md`

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
**Correction — research report relocated.**

The report has moved from `docs/research/` to **`archive/research/yt-dlp-js-runtime-and-pure-js-paths.md`**.

Rationale: `CLAUDE.md` designates `archive/` for notes and research materials, while `docs/` is reserved for normative project documentation (`CONTEXT.md`, `docs/adr/`, `docs/agents/`). A research report is the evidence behind a decision, not the decision itself — when this one is distilled into an ADR, that ADR is the normative artifact and cites the archived report.

title: Missing subtitles in the requested language
description:
## Question

What does `yt-transcript` do when a video has **no subtitles at all** in the requested language —
neither manually-authored nor auto-generated?

Hard error, or fall back to another language?

**Constrained by decisions already made:**

- The catalog is a pure function of `transcripts/`, so a bare "stub row in the catalog" is not
  reachable. Remembering such a video at all requires writing a real transcript file with real
  frontmatter — and the `subtitles` frontmatter key is settled as exactly `manual | auto`, with no
  third value.
- *Playlist and channel handling* settled the **detection** rule but deliberately not the policy:
  a fetch succeeded only if yt-dlp exited 0 **and** a non-empty subtitle file exists. Requesting a
  language that does not exist exits **0 with no error line and no file** (verified), so this
  condition is detectable but currently has no defined response.
- In a batch the video lands in the failure summary. The open question is what happens on the
  **single-video** path, and whether "no captions in `en`" should silently become "captions in `es`".

**Answer must state:** the single-video behaviour, the batch behaviour, whether any language
fallback happens and if so how the chosen language is surfaced to the user, and the exit code.
close_reason: Requested language is the output language: one blind yt-dlp invocation, auto-translation accepted, no cross-language fallback, hard error (exit 1) when no captions exist. manual|auto detected from <c> tags in the VTT body. 429 must be parsed from stderr since it also exits 0.

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
## Answer

**The requested language is the output language, always.** `yt-transcript` fetches the requested
language or it fails; it never writes a transcript in a language the user did not ask for.

### Fetch mechanics

One blind `yt-dlp` invocation per video — no `-J` pre-flight, no track ranking of our own:

```
--write-sub --write-auto-sub --sub-langs <lang>
```

**Verified:** when both a manual and an auto track exist for the same tag, yt-dlp writes exactly one
file and prefers the manual one (`rNxC16mlO60`, a TED talk with both: single `C.en.vtt`, zero `<c>`
tags — the manual track). The "prefer manual, fall back to auto" rule is therefore yt-dlp's default
behaviour and needs no code.

The tag is matched **exactly**. `--lang en` does not match `en-US` or `en-GB`. A video whose only
English is a human-authored `en-US` track reports "no subtitles" — accepted as a tail case; the error
names the video and the user re-runs with `--lang en-US`. `en-orig` is never requested: on an
English-original video `en` and `en-orig` are **byte-identical** (351,425 bytes both, `o3CX_Y59_74`).

`live_chat` is excluded from track selection. It is a JSON chat dump, not speech, and it is the only
"manual" track a live stream carries (`b4tE5aKhtlg`). yt-dlp's own help documents `all,-live_chat`
as the exclusion idiom, so this is idiomatic rather than a workaround.

### Auto-translation is accepted

YouTube auto-translates auto captions into ~160 languages, so "no subtitles in the requested
language" is nearly **unreachable** whenever a video has auto captions at all — `--sub-langs zu`
started downloading a Zulu track for an English video. A Spanish video (`_6N18g3ewnw`) lists
`es-orig`, `es` **and** `en`, where that `en` is machine-translated Spanish speech.

This is **accepted, not refused**: in practice the user is fetching English-language videos, and
where they are not, a translated English track is still the content they want. It records as
`subtitles: auto` like any other auto track. The frontmatter contract is **not** reopened — no eighth
key, no third `subtitles` value, no language field.

The consequence is deliberate: a transcript does not distinguish "English ASR" from "English
machine-translated from Spanish". That was weighed and waived.

### `manual` vs `auto` is read from the file, not the log

yt-dlp logs `Writing video subtitles to:` for auto tracks too (confirmed on `en-orig`), so the log is
not a discriminator. The **VTT body is**: auto tracks carry `<c>` word-timing tags and
`align:start position:0%` on every cue; manual tracks carry neither. Measured across all 8 auto files
in the repo (319–1265 `<c>` runs each) and the manual TED track (0 and 0). `Kind: captions` appears in
both and is useless.

**Rule:** presence of `<c>` word-timing tags ⇒ `auto`, absence ⇒ `manual`. Zero extra round trips, and
the cleaner already strips those tags.

### No usable subtitles

A video with no captions at all — captions disabled, music, live streams — is a **hard error**:
exit **1**, no file written, no catalog rebuild, message naming the video. There is nothing to fall
back to, and a stub row is unreachable anyway since the catalog is a pure function of `transcripts/`.

In a **batch** this is an ordinary member of the failure summary settled by *Playlist and channel
handling*: continue, collect, report, non-zero exit if any failed. Not special-cased, not retried —
it is permanent.

### HTTP 429 must be told apart from "no subtitles"

**Newly discovered, and it undercuts the settled success test.** A 429 on the subtitle download makes
yt-dlp print `ERROR: Unable to download video subtitles for 'en': HTTP Error 429: Too Many Requests`
and **still exit 0**, writing no file. Hit twice during this session. Exit code plus file existence —
the exact test *Playlist and channel handling* settled on — cannot distinguish a transient rate limit
from a permanently caption-less video.

**Rule:** parse stderr. `HTTP Error 429` / `Too Many Requests` ⇒ *rate-limited*, retried on the
already-settled 3-attempt 5s/15s/45s ladder. Any other empty result ⇒ *no subtitles*, permanent, no
retry. Without this a rate-limited batch reports a pile of videos as caption-less, and `--force` does
not help because the transcripts were never written in the first place.

### The four things the ticket asked for

- **Single-video:** requested language only; manual preferred by yt-dlp's default; nothing ⇒ hard error.
- **Batch:** ordinary entry in the failure summary; batch exits non-zero if any fetch failed.
- **Language fallback:** **none across languages.** Auto-translation *into* the requested language is
  accepted and is not a fallback — the output language is what the user asked for either way.
- **Exit code:** **1** for a single video with no usable subtitles; **0** when the transcript is written.

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
## Correction to the resolution above: the 429 rule

The resolution comment claims an HTTP 429 exits **0**, and builds a stderr-parsing rule on it. **That
measurement was wrong** — the `EXIT=0` I read was the exit status of `tail` at the end of a pipeline,
not yt-dlp's.

Measured directly, capturing yt-dlp's own status:

| Case | Exit | File | Log |
|---|---|---|---|
| No captions at all (`b4tE5aKhtlg`) | **0** | none | `[info] There are no subtitles for the requested languages` |
| HTTP 429 (`_6N18g3ewnw`, `p5nl9zD7_yk`) | **1** | none | `ERROR: Unable to download video subtitles for 'en': HTTP Error 429: Too Many Requests` |

**The exit code alone separates the permanent failure from the retryable one. No stderr parsing.**

This is simpler than what the resolution proposed, and it means the success test settled in *Playlist
and channel handling* — exit 0 **and** a non-empty subtitle file — stands **unchanged** rather than
being narrowed:

- exit 0, no file ⇒ **no subtitles**, permanent, hard error (exit 1 from `yt-transcript`), no retry.
- exit non-zero ⇒ a fetch failure; 429 remains the one case retried on the settled 5s/15s/45s ladder.

Everything else in the resolution stands. Sorry for the noise — the bad reading came from a pipeline,
and it was worth re-measuring because the whole rule hung on it.

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
## Follow-up: auto-translated tracks are effectively unobtainable

Attempting to verify the `<c>`-tag discriminator against a **third** class — an auto-*translated*
track, the class Q2(a) accepted — turned up something that bears on the decision itself.

**Every translated-track request returned HTTP 429. Every native-ASR request succeeded, in the same
minute, on the same videos.**

| Request | Track class | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `--sub-langs zu` on `o3CX_Y59_74` (English video) | translated | **429** — and this was the session's *first* subtitle download, before any load |
| `--sub-langs en` / `en-orig` on `o3CX_Y59_74` | native ASR | 351,425 bytes, exit 0 |
| `--sub-langs en` on `_6N18g3ewnw` (Spanish video) | translated | **429** ×3, including after a 4-minute cooldown |
| `--sub-langs es-orig` on `_6N18g3ewnw` | native ASR | exit 0, 375 `<c>` runs — *seconds after* the `en` request on the same video 429'd |
| `--sub-langs es` on `o3CX_Y59_74` | translated | **429** |
| `--sub-langs en` on `p5nl9zD7_yk` (Spanish video) | translated | **429** ×2 |

The first-request 429 rules out "I exhausted a quota by probing": YouTube appears to serve the
`tlang=` translation path under a separate and near-zero allowance for unauthenticated clients.

### What this means for the discriminator

The `<c>`-tag rule (tags ⇒ `auto`, none ⇒ `manual`) was verified against manual tracks (0 tags) and
native ASR tracks (319–1265 tags), and **remains unverified against translated tracks**. Since
translated tracks cannot be downloaded at all, every input the tool can actually receive falls into
one of the two verified classes. The rule is therefore sound for all reachable inputs — but the gap is
recorded here rather than papered over, and would need closing if the translation path ever opens up.

### What this means for Q2(a)

Accepting machine-translated captions was the right call on the merits, but it is **largely moot in
practice**: a non-English video fetched with the default `--lang en` will not yield a translation, it
will fail as *rate-limited*, burn the 3-attempt ladder, and report failure after ~65 seconds. Whether
that is the behaviour we want is a fresh question, raised as its own ticket.

title: Dedup safety on manually-authored subtitles
description:
## Question

Does the cleaner's `getOverlapSize` dedup step corrupt **manually-authored** subtitles?

The dedup logic assumes the rolling-window repetition that YouTube's auto-generated captions produce,
where each cue restates the tail of the previous one. Manual subtitles have no rolling window, so a
genuinely repeated phrase — "Yes. Yes.", a chorus, a deliberate restatement — could be silently
collapsed into one.

This matters now because manual subtitles are the **preferred** track, so this is the path taken
whenever it is available, and a silent deletion of real speech is exactly the failure a transcript
must not have.

Worth resolving with a prototype against real manual-subtitle input rather than by reading the code:
the question is empirical.

**Answer must state:** whether the corruption is real and under what input, and whether dedup is
skipped entirely on manual tracks, applied with different parameters, or left as-is with evidence
that it is safe.
close_reason: Dedup runs only on auto tracks; measured 13/13 false positives on 1504 manual cues, and no minimum-k separates the classes.

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
## Finding handed over from *Missing subtitles in the requested language* (ytdlp-sab.6)

A real manual-subtitle sample is now on hand and confirms this ticket's premise, plus surfaces a
second hazard it does not currently mention.

**Sample:** `rNxC16mlO60` (a TED talk), fetched with `--write-sub --sub-langs en`.

1. **The structural difference is confirmed and measurable.** Manual tracks carry **zero** `<c>`
   word-timing tags and **zero** `align:start position:0%` cue settings; all 8 auto files in this repo
   carry 319–1265 `<c>` runs each. The rolling-window restatement that `getOverlapSize` was written
   against is an artefact of the auto format and is simply absent here — so the dedup step is
   operating on input it was never designed for, exactly as this ticket suspects.

2. **New hazard: manual tracks open with non-speech credit cues.** The first cue of the sample is:

   ```
   00:00:00.000 --> 00:00:07.000
   Transcriber: isabella hilário
   Reviewer: Emma Gon
   ```

   This is not spoken content, and it would land at the top of the transcript body as prose. Worth
   deciding alongside the dedup question, since both are "what does the manual path do differently".

3. `Kind: captions` appears in **both** manual and auto headers and cannot be used to tell them apart.
   ytdlp-sab.6 settled the discriminator as the presence of `<c>` tags, which also gives this ticket a
   reliable way to know it is on the manual path.

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
## Answer

**The corruption is real, it is 100% false positives, and dedup is skipped entirely on manual tracks.**

### The corruption is real

`getOverlapSize` has **no minimum `k`**: it walks `k` from `min(len)` down to **1** and returns the
first match, comparing the head of the incoming cue against the tail of the **whole accumulated
paragraph**, not the previous cue.

Measured over **5 live-fetched manual VTTs, 1504 cues** (`rNxC16mlO60`, `iG9CE55wbtY`,
`8nHBGFKLHZQ`, `DxL2HoqLbyA`, `arj7oStGLkU` — all zero `<c>` tags), running the **settled**
pipeline (`PARAGRAPH_MIN_WORDS = 100`, sentence-end break, no timing), not the shipped 2.0s-pause one:

**13 deletions. All 13 are false positives. Zero true positives.** About one corruption per 115 cues.
Two of the five files (the shortest, 75 and 121 cues) had none, so short samples do not show it.

The recurring shapes:

| Shape | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| Sentence opens on the word the last one closed with | `…do that like that.` + `That would be the plan.` | `…that. would be the plan.` |
| Discourse marker | `…right now.` + `Now, sometimes…` | marker vanishes |
| Dialogue echo | `- Warmth.` + `- Warmth, light.` | `- Warmth. light.` |
| Rhetorical repetition | `…do you?` + `Do you?` | **whole cue erased** |
| Number split across cues | `…100 trillion,` + `trillion atoms…` | loses a magnitude |
| Quotation restated for emphasis | k=6 | six words gone |

The third and fourth rows are exactly the `Yes. Yes.` case the ticket hypothesised. This is not an
edge case: manual is the **preferred** track whenever it exists, so it is the common path.

### Retuning cannot fix it

| k | auto matches (genuine overlaps) | manual matches (all false) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 56 | 7 |
| 2 | 31 | 3 |
| 3 | 37 | 1 |
| 4 | 138 | 0 |
| 5 | 621 | 0 |
| 6 | 2001 | **1** |
| 7 | 3942 | **1** |
| 8–12 | 5734 | 0 |

Manual false positives reach **k=7**, inside auto's densest band. A minimum-`k` cutoff high enough to
kill them (≥8) would discard roughly **40%** of the genuine auto overlaps. The two classes are not
separable by any threshold on `k`.

### The decision

**Dedup runs only when the track is `auto`.** On a manual track the overlap is forced to 0:

```js
const overlap = subtitles === 'auto' ? getOverlapSize(para, words) : 0;
```

Justified twice over: dedup's true-positive count on manual input measured **0**, so skipping it
costs nothing, and its false-positive count measured 13, so skipping it is the whole fix.

**The classifier is already free.** The `<c>` word-timing rule settled in *Missing subtitles in the
requested language* (ytdlp-sab.6) is computed anyway to fill the `subtitles` frontmatter key. This is
the same signal with a second consumer — zero extra round trips, zero extra code.

**Ordering consequence for the spec:** classification stops being a labelling step that can happen
anywhere and becomes a **precondition of cleaning**. The VTT must be classified before the cue loop
runs, because the loop's behaviour now depends on the verdict. Both read the same file, so no extra
I/O — but the pipeline order is now load → classify → clean, and the spec must say so.

### Side observation — noted, not opened

Auto tracks also show low-`k` matches (56 at k=1, 31 at k=2, 37 at k=3 across 10,869 cues, ~0.5% of
auto matches) that are plausibly the same false positives, masked by the rolling window. Unmeasured.
The rolling window means auto cues genuinely do overlap, so a low-`k` match there is at least
plausible. Recorded here; deliberately **not** turned into a ticket or a fog patch.

### Prototype

Branch **`prototype/dedup-safety`** (commit `9a42655`):

- `prototype/dedup-safety/measure.mjs` — the measurement, verbatim `getOverlapSize`
- `prototype/dedup-safety/demo.built.html` — double-click: free-play plus all 13 real cases as tabs
- `prototype/dedup-safety/samples/` — the 5 manual VTTs
- `prototype/dedup-safety/FINDINGS.md` — the write-up

title: Shape and granularity of the spec hand-off
description:
## Question

What shape and granularity should the final hand-off take, so that **one implementer session** can
build `yt-transcript` end to end?

Every contract decision is now settled — fetching, output and filename, frontmatter, paragraphing,
catalog, playlist and channel handling. What remains is deciding how to present them.

Decide: whether the hand-off is a single spec ticket or several; how much of each closed ticket's
reasoning is restated versus linked; whether `CONTEXT.md` and the agent procedure doc are prerequisites
of the spec or products of the build; which decisions warrant an ADR (the bar being hard to reverse,
surprising without context, and the result of a real trade-off — the `watch?v=&list=` divergence from
yt-dlp's own default and the deliberate rejection of pure-JS fetching are the obvious candidates); and
what the implementer is expected to have on disk before starting.

Note the existing-artifact migration (7 `.vtt` files and their cleaned siblings at the repo root, plus
strays) is hand-off execution, not a decision — but the hand-off must say who does it and when.

**Answer must state:** the hand-off artifact list, what each contains, and which ADRs get written.

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
## A third ADR candidate, from *Missing subtitles in the requested language* (ytdlp-sab.6)

This ticket's question names two obvious ADR candidates — the `watch?v=&list=` divergence from
yt-dlp's default, and the rejection of pure-JS fetching. Here is a third, offered rather than written,
because choosing which decisions get an ADR is this ticket's call.

**Candidate: machine-translated captions are accepted and recorded as plain `auto`.**

YouTube auto-translates auto captions into ~160 languages, so fetching a Spanish video with the
default `--lang en` silently yields a machine translation of Spanish speech. That was weighed against
rejecting translated tracks and against marking them, and **accepting them unmarked won** — the
frontmatter's seven keys stay closed, and in practice the videos being fetched are English anyway.

Against the three bars:

- **Hard to reverse:** yes. Marking translations later means an eighth frontmatter key *and* every
  transcript already on disk is unmarked and indistinguishable.
- **Surprising without context:** yes. `subtitles: auto` on a transcript of a Spanish video reads as
  an error until you know it was a deliberate choice.
- **A real trade-off:** yes. Three alternatives were on the table and the cost of the winner — a
  transcript cannot say what language was actually spoken — was accepted with eyes open.

Passes all three. `CONTEXT.md`'s **Subtitle track** entry has already been amended to carry the
consequence, so an ADR would be recording the *why*, not the *what*.

title: Translated tracks are rate-limited into uselessness
description:
## Question

Auto-translated caption tracks **reliably return HTTP 429** while native tracks download fine in the
same minute (evidence: resolution thread on *Missing subtitles in the requested language*,
ytdlp-sab.6 — six requests across three videos, including a 429 on the session's very first subtitle
download, before any load). YouTube appears to serve the `tlang=` translation path under a separate,
near-zero allowance for unauthenticated clients.

*Missing subtitles in the requested language* settled two rules that now collide on this input:

- Auto-translation into the requested language is **accepted** — so fetching a Spanish video with the
  default `--lang en` is a supported path.
- **429 is the one retried failure** (3 attempts, 5s/15s/45s), because it was reasoned about as
  transient.

Together they mean a non-English video fetched with default settings spends ~65 seconds retrying
something that will not succeed, then reports *rate-limited* — an accurate but useless diagnosis, since
the user's real options are to pass `--lang <original>` or give up.

Decide: whether a 429 on a **translated** track is still treated as transient and retried, or
recognised as the effectively-permanent condition it appears to be; whether the tool detects this case
at all (it would have to know the track it asked for is a translation, which it currently does not,
having deliberately dropped the `-J` pre-flight); and what the error tells the user — in particular
whether it should name the video's original language and suggest `--lang <orig>`.

Note the cheap version needs no pre-flight: the failure message could simply mention that a requested
language absent from the video's own audio is served by a heavily throttled endpoint, and suggest
`--list-subs`.

**Answer must state:** the retry behaviour for this case, how (or whether) it is distinguished from an
ordinary 429, and the wording and exit code the user sees.
close_reason: Resolved: no special-casing. English is the scope, so the original language is never surfaced and no translation-aware diagnosis is built. Retry ladder, exit code 1 and the failure message all stand unchanged.

## Resolution: nothing is special-cased. The settled rules already cover this input.

The ticket asked whether a 429 on a **translated** track should be told apart from an ordinary 429,
whether the tool should detect the case at all, and what the user is told. The answer to all three is
the minimal one, and it follows from a scope decision the ticket had not registered.

### The scope decision that settles it

**The tool retrieves English subtitles.** Manual or auto, authored or machine-translated — any of them
is acceptable output, and the tool never asks what language the video was spoken in. A video with no
English track of its own is served by YouTube's translation endpoint; if that endpoint refuses, the
fetch fails, and retrying later is the **user's** call. The original language is not interesting, is
never surfaced, and is never suggested as an alternative.

This rules out the ticket's own proposed remedies: naming the video's original language, suggesting
`--lang <orig>`, and any form of translation-aware diagnosis. There is no audience for that advice.

### The three things the answer must state

**1. Retry behaviour: unchanged.** A 429 stays the one retried failure, on the already-settled
3-attempt 5s/15s/45s ladder. A non-English video fetched with the default `--lang en` therefore spends
~65 seconds on a request that will very likely not succeed. **That cost is accepted.** Shortening the
ladder was considered and rejected: it would trade resilience on genuine transient limits — the case
the ladder exists for — against a faster dead end on a path the user is content to abandon anyway.

**2. Distinguished from an ordinary 429: not at all.** The tool cannot tell them apart and will not
try. The `-J` pre-flight is dropped by deliberate decision, so at the moment of failure a
translated-track 429 and a genuine rate limit are the **same observable**: exit non-zero,
`HTTP Error 429`, no file. Two ways of buying the distinction back were considered and rejected —

- *Eager pre-flight* (`-J` before every download): taxes every fetch, including the overwhelming
  majority that are native English and never reach this path, and reopens a settled decision.
- *Lazy probe* (`--list-subs` only after the retries are exhausted): costs nothing on the happy path,
  but its entire payoff is the original-language diagnosis that the scope decision above discards.

With nothing downstream of the distinction, the distinction is not worth its cost in either form.

**3. What the user sees: exit 1, and the existing rate-limited message.** No new exit code. A second
non-zero code (permanent vs. retryable-later) was considered and rejected: there is no scripting
consumer in scope, and an exit-status vocabulary is a public contract that is cheap to add later and
awkward to change. The distinction, such as it is, lives in the message text.

The message names the video and reports that the subtitle download was rate-limited after 3 attempts,
and says a later run may succeed. It does **not** speculate about translation, the original language,
or `--lang`.

In a **batch** this is an ordinary member of the failure summary settled by *Playlist and channel
handling* (ytdlp-sab.4): continue, collect, report, non-zero exit if any fetch failed.

### Considered and dropped

- **Never requesting a translated track at all** (fail immediately with "no `en` subtitles" instead of
  429-ing for 65 seconds). Cleaner in isolation, but wrong here: a machine-translated English track is
  *exactly* the output the user wants when it can be had. Declining to ask for it would convert a
  sometimes-succeeding path into a never-succeeding one. Not pursued, and the research into whether
  `yt-dlp` can even express that distinction was not commissioned.
- **Consecutive-429 bail-out in a batch** (abandon the batch once N fetches in a row are rate-limited,
  instead of burning ~65s per video). Reached the point of being ticketed separately, then dropped on
  the same reasoning as the ladder: the user's remedy for a rate-limited run is to run it again later,
  and a batch that fails every member reports exactly that. Not ticketed.

### One fact the spec should not misstate

"Try again later" is the user's option, not a promise the tool makes, and the retry ladder is not a
wait-for-it-to-heal mechanism. The translation endpoint returned 429 on a session's **first** subtitle
request, before any load, and again after a four-minute cooldown, while native-track downloads on the
same videos succeeded in the same minute (evidence: follow-up thread on *Missing subtitles in the
requested language*, ytdlp-sab.6). It behaves like a near-zero standing allowance for unauthenticated
clients, not an exhausted quota that refills. The message should therefore say a later run *may*
succeed, and claim nothing stronger.
